name: Jill Feldman
summary: Jill Feldman was diagnosed with lung cancer in 2009, at age 39.
The Patient Story, in a 10 January 2025 interview, lists the cancer as stage 1A, with an EGFR exon 19 deletion.
In her own words in that interview, she said she was EGFR-positive.
She wrote in June 2020 that she took erlotinib after her first surgery, even though it was not standard care.
She named her oncologist, Phil Bonomi, in that post.
She wrote that the drug worked until she stopped taking it. A new nodule appeared eight months later.
As of 10 January 2025, she described a later progression in the spring, radiation to that area, and staying on the same treatment.
She did not name that later drug in the January 2025 interview we opened.
We found no first-person update from her in 2026 about her scans or her drug.

actions.what: A lung nodule watched for three and a half years grew
actions.quote: My scans were not concerning until 2009, when a nodule we had been following for three and a half years became aggressive, and I was diagnosed with lung cancer at 39 years old.

actions.what: Surgery: early lung cancer (stage Ia) with an EGFR gene change
actions.quote: I had surgery and was diagnosed with stage Ia adenocarcinoma, positive for an EGFR mutation (EGFR & KRAS were all they tested for).
date_basis: My scans were not concerning until 2009

milestone.quote: I had surgery and was diagnosed with stage Ia adenocarcinoma, positive for an EGFR mutation

label_basis.quote: I was diagnosed with lung cancer at 39 years old.

phases.title: A pill after surgery
phases.span_note: Her 2020 post gives no year for this.

actions.what: Erlotinib (off label) as extra treatment after surgery
actions.quote: Even though the cancer was stage Ia, I knew I was at risk for recurrence. I didn’t want my kids to ever go through what I went through, so I took Erlotinib (off label) as adjuvant therapy.
date_basis: My oncologist (Phil Bonomi) knew I wanted adjuvant therapy after my first surgery, even though it wasn’t standard of care.

actions.what: She wrote that it worked until she stopped taking it
actions.quote: And it worked…. until I stopped taking it.
actions.date_note: Her 2020 post gives no dates for this.

phases.title: The cancer came back
phases.span_note: Her 2020 post counts months, not years, here.

actions.what: A new nodule on her scan
actions.quote: Eight months after I stopped taking Erlotinib there was a new nodule on my scan, and four months later I had surgery to remove it, another stage Ia EGFR mutant lung cancer.

actions.what: Second surgery removed it: another early EGFR lung cancer
actions.quote: Eight months after I stopped taking Erlotinib there was a new nodule on my scan, and four months later I had surgery to remove it, another stage Ia EGFR mutant lung cancer.

milestone.quote: Eight months after I stopped taking Erlotinib there was a new nodule on my scan, and four months later I had surgery to remove it, another stage Ia EGFR mutant lung cancer.

actions.what: New growth on scans; the same disease, still in her chest
actions.quote: The surgery was successful, but unfortunately, there was new tumor growth on my post-op scan, and even more on my next scan. I was lucky the cancer was contained to my chest, but after looking closer at the pathology of the two resections we learned it was the same disease and not a new primary.

phases.title: Focused radiation when needed
phases.span_note: From early 2013; it ended “last year” in her post of 12 June 2020, so 2019.

actions.what: Chose focused radiation to the lung spots (SBRT)
actions.quote: Erlotinib was still the only TKI approved for EGFR mutant lung cancer in early 2013. SBRT for intrapulmonary metastasis wasn’t a thing, but risks were low, so my care team and I decided it was a better option for me rather than going back on Erlotinib.

actions.what: Focused radiation as needed: wait, watch, treat
actions.quote: I was willing to take the risk and was fortunate to use SBRT as needed for five years.

phases.title: Back on a targeted pill
phases.span_note: “Last year” in her 12 June 2020 post; status from her interview of 10 January 2025.

actions.quote: Going back on a TKI was definitely a hard pill to swallow (literally), but it was the first time in 10 years I was not overcome with fear.
date_basis: The wait, watch, treat with local therapy as needed approach ended last year when one nodule continued to misbehave. Nothing else was imminent, but SBRT was risky because of the location of the nodule. It was time to treat the disease, not the scan.
actions.date_note: “Last year” in her post of 12 June 2020, so 2019.

actions.what: Cancer grew in one area; radiation there, staying on the same treatment
actions.quote: That just happened to me in the spring. I had progression, and I ended up being able to radiate the area where the cancer was growing. Now, I stay on the same treatment, which is so important to be able to do that and get more mileage out of that treatment.

phase_links.cause: She knew she was at risk of it coming back. Her oncologist asked her “What are your goals?” She said she needed to live to raise her children, and he recommended the pill.

sources.quote: Even though the cancer was stage Ia, I knew I was at risk for recurrence. I didn’t want my kids to ever go through what I went through, so I took Erlotinib (off label) as adjuvant therapy.
But, let me ask you a question: What are your goals?
I just need to do everything in my power to live to raise my children.
Without hesitation he said, “I recommend you take Erlotinib as adjuvant therapy”.
